1203.dq: At the lexical level prominence is realized by stress so that prominent syllables have no lexically specified F0. At the postlexical level, prominence is realized cumlinatively, marking the head of a trochaic foot. ... Primary stress generally falls on the leftmost or only heavy syllable in a word
1203.dloc: Gooden 2007, section 1 'Introduction', p. 1, and section 2 'JC STRESS', p. 2, of the 9-page workshop paper (rendered from the PDF); APiCS survey 8, section 4
1203.heavy: coda consonants, long vowels and diphthongs contribute to syllable weight
1203.prule: Weight-sensitive, trochaic: primary stress on the leftmost (or only) heavy syllable of the word (heavy = long vowel, diphthong, or coda consonant); if the word has no heavy syllable, primary stress is penultimate (final light syllables unstressed). Stated with 'generally' and 'a small percentage of the data have alternate stress patterns'; author also calls JC stress 'phonologically contrastive'.
1203.srule: Secondary stress falls two syllables away from the main stress (trochaic feet): ˈkaŋ.kan.ˌtar, ˌba.da.ˈrie.ʃan, ˌpo.ko.ˈmie.nja; word-final light syllables are not stressed (no secondary in ˈniiz.bɛ.rɪ). [Gooden 2003 ch. 5, pp. 153, 163, 168 adds: none in disyllables; never on a word-final light syllable.]
1203.quote: Stress in JC is phonologically contrastive. This supports previous analyses of JC stress, (Wells 1973, Alderete 1993, Gooden 2003). ... JC has a weight-sensitive stress system with coda consonants, long vowels and diphthongs contributing to syllable weight (cf. Alderete 1993, Gooden 2003, Gooden, in press). The preferred foot type in JC stress assignment is a trochee. Primary stress generally falls on the leftmost or only heavy syllable in a word and secondary stress falls two syllables away from the main stress as shown in (1). (1) pa.ˈlaav ‘to lie about idly’, ˈpai.zn̩ ‘poison’, ˈgaa.lɪn ‘e…

1203.exq_: This generalization is consistent for bisyllabic, trisyllabic and quadrasyllabic words. A small percentage of the data have alternate stress patterns (see Gooden 2003 for a detailed analysis).
1203.tone: Not a tone language per this source: no lexically specified F0; postlexical pitch accents (H*, H+L*) dock on primary-stressed syllables, boundary tones H%/L% at phrase edges (AM analysis).

morph.stmt: The APiCS sketch presents Jamaican as an essentially isolating creole: tense, aspect, mood and negation are free preverbal particles ("the preverbal anterior marker wehn"; "a number of preverbal modal markers"; order "mood > tense > aspect"), the articles stand "at the left edge of the phrase", the one grammatical marker that follows its host is the NP-level plural dem "which is placed after the noun", and the only word-level affixation it describes is on pronouns ("prefixing the preposition fi to the personal pronouns, e.g. fi-yu 'yours'"; "affixing the reflexive morpheme -self to the personal pronouns"), beside compounding (man-/uman- gender compounds) and reduplication — so what little…

1204.prule: No reached source states where main stress falls in simplex words. Westin 1897 (the primary phonetic key for Jämtland) describes three tonal accents (akut, grav, cirkumflex) 'på tonstafvelsen (den starka stafvelsen)', i.e. presupposes a stressed syllable, marks its position word by word in transcription, but gives no placement rule; Germanic root/initial stress is implicit (fàra, skràmal, óstn all initial) but never stated. The only positional statements are sub-dialectal and about compounds: Westin p.9 and Flemström p.2 both say East Jämtland (Ragunda/Fors/Håsjö/Hällesjö) puts the stress on the last member of a compound (kaffepanna -> kaffePANNa, dagaman -> dagaMAN; Flemström hedges it as 'benägenheten... på någon av de sista stavelserna', all examples compounds), whereas central Jamtska stresses the first member with grave vs. acute accent (dàɣamán, káfapàn). Otherwise: accent 1/2 tonal contrast, two-peak circumflex on apocopated old long-stem disyllables in central Jamtska/Offerdal (absent in the east and in Bergsmålet), partial retention of Old Norse short stressed syllables. Not a syllable-count rule; hence not determinable from the sources (sources reached, silent on simplex stress position).

tn.translation: The accents on the tone-syllable (the strong syllable) are three, namely: ´ acute, e.g. óst, óstn (cheese, the cheese). This accent usually need not be written. ` grave and high tone, e.g. fàra ... in which words the first, properly accented syllable is followed by one with higher tone. ... ^ circumflex, occurs very often in Central Jamtish and is placed over a vowel that has two accents or seems to stand for two vowels, e.g. kâst 'throw', read as kàast ... This accent must always be written; compare e.g. mat 'food', mat 'faint, tired', both with unwritten acute, and mât 'mat'.

1205.dq: The clearest phonological criterion for wordhood is stress. Stress is by default word-final, and words have at most one stress. Most function words, including linkers (§25.1.6), determiners (§9.1), postpositions (§8.2) and even relator nouns (§8.3) lack stress (unless they receive special emphasis).
1205.dloc: sect. 3.7 Suprasegmentals, p. 68; sect. 3.8.1 Wordhood, pp. 68-69; sect. 11.2.3 Stress, p. 480 (2nd-ed. pagination; pp. 102-103, 514)
1205.prule: One stress per phonological word, by default on the word-final syllable, which for verbs is the last syllable of the verb STEM: person-indexation suffixes (slots +1..+4) and the peg suffix -ci are never stressed (giving surface penultimate/antepenultimate stress in suffixed verb forms), and three prefixes (inverse -wɣ-, negative sensory mɯ́j-, interrogative ɯ́-) attract stress; comitative adverb derivation also shifts stress; a handful of function words (kɯ́nɤ, cínɤ, nóʁmɯz, kóʁmɯz) have penultimate stress. Author's own label: 'morphologically determined stress'. No weight conditioning; no tone.
1205.srule: None: 'Phonological words only have one stress' (§3.7); 'words have at most one stress' (§3.8.1). Only bipartite verbs (two merged conjugated verb forms) have 'two stresses, one on each verb stem' (§11.6.3, p. 492); ideophone initial emphatic stress 'is not phonologically distinctive' (§3.7).
1205.quote: Japhug has no tonal contrasts. However, there is morphologically determined stress. Phonological words only have one stress, which is located by default on the final syllable of the word (§3.8.1, §11.6.1). The personal agreement suffixes (§14.2.1, §11.3) and the peg suffix -ci (§11.4) never receive stress, and their vowels are optionally devoiced. ... Stress can be antepenultimate in the case of verb forms with two suffixes as in to-k-ɤmɯ-rpú-ndʑi-ci ‘they bumped into each other’ (ifr-peg-recip-bump-du-peg). There are only three verbal prefixes which can attract stress: the inverse -wɣ- (§14.…
1205.loc: sect. 3.7 Suprasegmentals, p. 68; sect. 3.8.1 Wordhood, pp. 68-69; sect. 11.2.3 Stress, p. 480 (2nd-ed. pagination; pp. 102-103, 514)
1205.idn: Japhug (local name kɯrɯskɤt), 'almost exclusively' the dialect of kɤmɲɯ village (Kamnyu) (a named variety of the language); data: Kamnyu (kɤmɲɯ) village, Mbarkham county, Rngaba prefecture, Sichuan, China; author's own fieldwork on nine trips…
1205.exq_: There are only three groups of exceptions to word-final stress placement (for instance the unstressed suffix -ndʑi in 1), as seen in the previous section (§3.7). Given its predictability, stress is not noted in the transcription employed in this grammar, except on stress-attracting prefixes.
1205.tone: 'Unlike all other Gyalrong languages... Japhug has no tonal contrasts'; 'Japhug lacks tonal alternations'. Stress, not tone/pitch accent; author notes 'the almost complete loss of contrastive stress (§3.7)'.

1209.prule: Final syllable stressed if it contains a long vowel or ends in a consonant cluster (incl. final geminate); otherwise penultimate, regardless of penult weight. Anaptyctic vowels do not count. 1210.prule: Three level tonemes (High, Mid, Low) plus falling and rising glides, lexically and grammatically contrastive. 1211.prule: Word stress position is not predictable (lexical); penultimate is the most frequent position, final and antepenultimate also occur; stress confined to the last three syllables; oxytones usually end in -r/-l/-s or a nasal vowel, proparoxytones are mostly recent introductions; verbs: penult on the bare base, final base vowel before a desinence (-ba etc.) or an enclitic pronoun. Stress realised mainly by intensity (plus length when non-final).
1211.srule: Word-initial secondary stress: in words where more than one syllable precedes the tonic, the initial syllable carries a secondary stress, clearly distinct from the fully unstressed syllables adjacent to the tonic (brìnkadjon, làbrador, nòbidádi, pàpelinhu, ràpariga); not marked in the official orthography. Nothing is said for words with a single pretonic syllable; no alternating/rhythmic stresses are described.

evidence_works.detail: Method: a stress count over the words of three sample texts, 'num total de 461 palavras, das quais 197 são monossilábicas' (p. 108), with function words and stressed monosyllables excluded (p. 109). Findings for Fogo: two stress positions only, 'O foguense apresenta dois tipos de acentuação. A oxítona... e a paroxítona... A acentuação proparoxítona é inexistente no meu corpus.' (p. 108); '68% das palavras da língua apresentam uma acentuação paroxítona' and 'A acentuação oxítona tem uma prevalência de 32% na língua' (pp. 109-110); nouns and adjectives predominantly paroxytone, the oxytone nouns 'apresentando sílabas finais fechadas por consoantes ou ditongos, que determinam a atração do acento para a última sílaba' (p. 111); verbs 'sempre oxítonos na forma livre e paroxítonos em formas flexionadas' with suffixes -ba, -du and object clitics ([el oˈdʒaba], [el oˈdʒadu], p. 111). For Santiago it only restates Quint (2000: 39): '91% de acentuação paroxítona, contra 9% de acentuação oxítona' and 'a quase totalidade (99%) das palavras de padrão C(C)Vx2 são paroxítonas' (p. 113), and Quint (2001, 2008b) for the verb shift 'onde a acentuação paroxítona é o padrão para todas as classes gramaticais' (p. 112); these Santiago figures are secondhand. Internal tension in the thesis: §5.2 says adjectives 'pode ser oxítono, paroxítono ou proparoxítono, preenchendo os três paradigmas acentuais existentes na língua' (p. 120), against ch. 4's 'inexistente no meu corpus'.

1216.prule: Lexical (word-level, isolation-form) stress 'usually' on the FINAL SYLLABLE OF THE STEM (Bridgeman 1961:333). Her illustrating pairs ejuvi 'you strangle something' / eju-vi 'you come here for a short time' and ajepota 'I light a fire' / ajepo-ta 'I will jump' set a monomorphemic stem (word-final stress) against stem + suffix (-vi 'for a short time', -ta future; stress on the stem-final syllable before the suffix), so the surface position in the word depends on morphological make-up; p. 334 further lists the purposive haqã as 'unstressed' in its isolation form. Loan words 'and some apparently native words' have penult stress (háša 'hatchet', ója 'kettle', áva 'man'). In connected discourse a separate sentence stress (″) and rhythm perturb lexical stress ('In context lexical stress is sometimes perturbed'; 'rhythm is of primary importance in the determination of stress placement'; 'Alternate stress placement appears to be controlled by the rhythm pattern').

Similarly, downstep is underlyingly a high tone lowered by a preceding unassociated low tone in Kalaḅarị.

1222.prule: Stress is the contrastive (phonemic) suprasegmental of Kamano: the position of the (first) stress is lexically specified and distinguishes minimal pairs (ka'na 'heavy' vs 'kana 'road'; ka'fa 'rat' vs 'kafa 'door'; ka'raƀe 'shell' vs kara'ƀe 'tree kangaroo'), including final-syllable stress in disyllables (the stress mark precedes the affected syllable throughout the paper, cf. Gahuku 'musi vs mu'si). Young describes the first stress as falling on the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th or 5th syllable and states only that 'The final, sixth, syllable is never stressed' (the sixth syllable of a maximal word), not a general ban on word-final stress.
1222.srule: Young 1962: one degree of stress intensity; a word has one or two stresses. Revised by the later SIL descriptions (Drew 1963 sec. 7; Payne & Drew 1970 p. 1): non-pertinent stresses fall on alternate syllables both before and after the lexical (pertinent) stress, skipping -gaha, -'ne and the vowel a-umlaut; a preceding rhythmic stress is as strong as the pertinent one, following ones much lighter.

morph.rootq: "Stress or accent is phonemic. There is one important stress to each word and from that point both forwards and backwards each alternate syllable is stressed, unless it should fall on the future tense marker -gaha, past tense marker -'ne or the vowel ä. 1224.dq: A prosodic stem consists of a strong syllable and all the prosodically weak syllables that follow it. In other words, a prosodic stem is a unit that runs from the beginning of one prosodically strong syllable to the beginning of the next one. ... 1224.prule: Stress-like 'prosodic prominence' (strong vs weak syllables) is lexically specified for every syllable; the default is stem-initial prominence: the first syllable with an onset of a morphological stem (noun/verb/adjective/adverb) is usually strong, stem-initial vowels/syllabic nasals ('prosodic prefixes', subject indexes 1SG) are weak, non-initial stem syllables are weak (lenited onsets). Cues: longer onset/vowel duration, greater loudness (impressionistic), fuller segmental and tonal contrast inventory in strong syllables; pitch is NOT a cue (tone language).
1224.srule: Not mentioned in Lesage 2020, ch. 4 'Prosodic prominence' (pp. 95-116 read): prominence is a binary strong/weak opposition with no ranking among strong syllables; some lexemes carry more than one (unranked, lexically listed) prosodic peak (§4.3.3).

1229.tone: Kikaonde is tonal: 'Kikaonde has two tonemes, high (H) and low (L)' (p.7); tone is lexical, morphological and syntactic (p.8). Wright states 'Kaonde stress is independent of tone. tn.quote: The actual musical pitch of the individual syllables may be very varied and complex, but the significant contrasts that affect meaning are only two. We may say that Kikaonde has two tonemes, high (H) and low (L). In this outline high tones will be marked with an accent (´) and low tones left unmarked. The tone is marked on the vowel of the syllable or on the homorganic nasal, if it is syllabic. Long vowels may be considered as a sequence of two short vowels; accordingly they may be recorded as: level high (HH) ... level low (LL) ... rising (LH) ... falling (HL)
tn.cite: Wright, J.L. 2007 [1977]. An Outline of Kikaonde Grammar. Series ed. M.E. Kashoki. Lusaka: Bookworld Publishers and UNZA Press.
tn.note: Two level tonemes H/L on each syllable; rising and falling only on long vowels as LH/HL sequences. Separate weak word stress, independent of tone except that a final high-toned syllable is stressed.
